title: Propulsion
tagline: Thrust and efficiency, gas-turbine cycles, inlets and nozzles, compressors, turbines and combustors, propellers, and rocket propulsion
summary: Propulsion systems produce the thrust that moves aircraft and spacecraft. The course derives thrust and efficiencies from momentum and energy balances, analyses turbojet, turbofan, turboprop and ramjet cycles and their components — inlets, nozzles, compressors, combustors and turbines — and treats propellers and, at textbook level, rocket propulsion: the rocket equation, nozzle performance and chemical and electric rockets.
overview: Propulsion is the branch of aerospace engineering that deals with the production of thrust. Every aircraft and spacecraft needs a propulsion system to overcome drag, climb, accelerate, or change orbit, and the design of that system governs the size, weight, cost and performance of the entire vehicle. This course develops the thermodynamic, fluid-mechanical and combustion principles that underlie every practical propulsion device, from the turboprop that powers a regional airliner to the liquid-hydrogen engine that lifts a launch vehicle out of Earth's gravity well.

The course begins with the momentum and energy balances that define thrust, specific fuel consumption and the three efficiencies — thermal, propulsive and overall — that measure how well a propulsion system converts chemical energy into useful work. It then works through the gas-turbine engine cycle, showing how pressure ratio, turbine inlet temperature and bypass ratio determine efficiency and thrust, and how the Brayton cycle is modified by real-component losses.

The middle chapters treat the individual components of a gas-turbine engine: inlets and nozzles that manage the airflow entering and leaving the engine, compressors that raise the pressure, combustors that add heat, and turbines that extract work to drive the compressor and fan. Each component is analysed with the tools used in preliminary design — one-dimensional compressible flow, velocity triangles and the Euler turbomachinery equation, non-dimensional loading and flow coefficients, and performance maps.

The final chapters extend the analysis to propellers, where momentum and blade-element theories predict thrust and efficiency, and to rockets, where the Tsiolkovsky equation governs the velocity increment achievable with a given mass of propellant. The rocket chapters cover nozzle theory, propellant selection, staging, and electric propulsion, providing a complete picture of how vehicles are propelled from the runway to orbit and beyond.
outcomes: Derive the thrust equation from a control-volume momentum balance and apply it to air-breathing and rocket engines.
Analyse ideal and real Brayton cycles for turbojets, turbofans, turboprops and ramjets, and compute thermal, propulsive and overall efficiencies.
Design subsonic and supersonic inlets and convergent-divergent nozzles, and compute their pressure recovery and thrust coefficients.
Apply the Euler turbomachinery equation and velocity triangles to axial and centrifugal compressors and axial turbines, and interpret compressor maps.
Size a combustor from the fuel-air ratio, residence time and pressure-drop constraints, and evaluate combustion efficiency and emissions.
Use momentum and blade-element theories to predict propeller thrust, power and efficiency, and select the advance ratio for maximum efficiency.
Apply the Tsiolkovsky equation to single- and multi-stage rockets, compute specific impulse and mass ratio, and select propellants for a given mission.
Evaluate rocket nozzle performance (thrust coefficient, characteristic velocity, expansion ratio) and compare chemical and electric propulsion systems.

chapters.title: Thrust and propulsive efficiency
chapters.summary: Thrust from a momentum balance, specific fuel consumption and specific impulse, and thermal, propulsive and overall efficiencies.

chapters.title: Gas-turbine engine cycles
chapters.summary: Ideal and real cycle analysis of turbojets, turbofans, turboprops and ramjets.

chapters.title: Inlets and nozzles
chapters.summary: Subsonic and supersonic inlets, convergent and convergent–divergent nozzles, and their losses.

chapters.title: Compressors
chapters.summary: Velocity triangles and the Euler turbomachinery equation, axial and centrifugal compressors, stage loading, stall and surge.

chapters.title: Turbines
chapters.summary: Axial turbine stages, blade loading and cooling, and matching the turbine to the compressor.

chapters.title: Combustors
chapters.summary: Combustion chamber design, flame stabilisation, combustion efficiency and pollutant emissions.

chapters.title: Propellers
chapters.summary: Momentum and blade-element theories of propellers, propeller efficiency, and the choice between propellers and fans.

chapters.title: Rocket propulsion fundamentals
chapters.summary: The rocket equation and staging, the thrust coefficient and characteristic velocity of rocket nozzles.

chapters.title: Chemical and electric rockets
chapters.summary: Liquid, solid and hybrid rocket engines and electric propulsion, compared at the level of performance and system design.

history.title: John Barber's gas-turbine patent
history.detail: John Barber's British patent describes a machine in which gas from a heated producer is compressed, burned and directed at a turbine wheel — the earliest recorded statement of the gas-turbine idea, far ahead of the materials needed to make it work.

history.title: Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation
history.detail: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky publishes his study of space travel by reaction devices, with the logarithmic relation between velocity increment and mass ratio that bears his name.

history.title: The Wright Flyer's propellers
history.detail: On 17 December 1903 the Wright Flyer makes the first controlled, sustained powered flights, driven by two propellers that the Wrights designed by treating the blades as rotating wings, using their own wind-tunnel data.

history.title: First liquid-propellant rocket
history.detail: On 16 March 1926 at Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard launches a rocket burning gasoline and liquid oxygen; the flight lasts about 2.5 seconds.

history.title: Whittle's first engine runs
history.detail: Frank Whittle's experimental turbojet, built by Power Jets, first runs on a test bed on 12 April 1937.

history.title: First jet-powered flight
history.detail: The Heinkel He 178, powered by Hans von Ohain's centrifugal-flow turbojet, makes the first flight of a jet-propelled aircraft on 27 August 1939.

history.title: Sputnik 1 reaches orbit
history.detail: On 4 October 1957 an R-7 launcher — a core stage with four strap-on boosters — places the 83.6 kg Sputnik 1 in Earth orbit, the first practical demonstration of staging to orbital velocity.

history.title: First flight of the Saturn V
history.detail: Five F-1 gas-generator-cycle engines, each producing about 6.7 MN of thrust at sea level, power the first stage of the Saturn V on its first flight; the F-1 remains the most powerful single-chamber liquid-propellant engine flown.

history.title: High-bypass turbofans enter airline service
history.detail: The Boeing 747 enters service in January 1970 with Pratt & Whitney JT9D engines, putting the high-bypass turbofan — large fan, slow jet, high propulsive efficiency — into everyday use.

history.title: Deep Space 1 flies on an ion engine
history.detail: NASA's Deep Space 1, launched on 24 October 1998, is the first spacecraft to use a gridded xenon ion thruster (NSTAR) as its primary propulsion.

references.title: Mechanics and Thermodynamics of Propulsion
references.authors: P. G. Hill and C. R. Peterson
references.note: 2nd edition (Addison-Wesley). The classic unified treatment of thrust, cycles, turbomachinery, combustion and rockets; the model for most of this course.

references.title: Elements of Propulsion: Gas Turbines and Rockets
references.note: AIAA Education Series. Parametric (on-design) and performance (off-design) cycle analysis with worked examples; source of the MIL-E-5007D inlet-recovery schedule used here.

references.title: Gas Turbine Theory
references.authors: H. I. H. Saravanamuttoo, G. F. C. Rogers, H. Cohen, P. V. Straznicky and A. C. Nix
references.note: 7th edition (Pearson). Real cycles, component design and off-design matching of gas turbines, with an industrial perspective.

references.title: Aircraft Propulsion
references.note: 2nd edition (Wiley). Broad modern textbook covering inlets, nozzles, turbomachinery, combustors and propellers, with many exercises.

references.title: Fluid Mechanics and Thermodynamics of Turbomachinery
references.authors: S. L. Dixon and C. A. Hall
references.note: 7th edition (Butterworth-Heinemann). The standard reference for velocity triangles, stage loading, efficiency correlations and centrifugal machines.

references.title: Gas Turbine Combustion: Alternative Fuels and Emissions
references.authors: A. H. Lefebvre and D. R. Ballal
references.note: 3rd edition (CRC Press). Combustor design, flame stabilisation, combustion efficiency and pollutant formation.

references.title: Rocket Propulsion Elements
references.authors: G. P. Sutton and O. Biblarz
references.note: 9th edition (Wiley). The standard rocket textbook: nozzle theory, liquid, solid and hybrid propulsion and electric propulsion at the system level.

references.title: Fundamentals of Electric Propulsion: Ion and Hall Thrusters
references.authors: D. M. Goebel and I. Katz
references.note: Wiley / JPL Space Science and Technology Series. Physics and engineering of gridded ion and Hall thrusters.
